title: Families assemble changing care portfolios, but affordability, trust and work design separate the care they use from the care they want
source_unit: Center for the Study of Social Policy, The Care Families Use, The Care Families Want: How Policy Can Better Support the Care of Young Children, September 2026
geography: United States; qualitative research in Massachusetts, North Carolina and New Mexico, with parents and primary caregivers across rural, small-city and metropolitan settings

observations.period: May-November 2024 interviews; how families actually organize young-child care

portfolio_care.value: most interviewed parents relied on multiple care arrangements simultaneously or sequentially as needs and circumstances changed

care_types.value: care portfolios combined parental care, formal early care and education, and family, friend or neighbor care

use_want_gap.value: the care arrangements and sequencing families wanted often differed from what they could achieve in practice

observations.method: More than 70 qualitative interviews with parents, primary caregivers, family members, friends and early-childhood educators; 51 parent or primary-caregiver interviews are central to the report.
observations.uncertainty: The purposive qualitative sample is designed to reveal mechanisms and lived sequences, not estimate national prevalence or represent all U.S. families.
observations.subgroup: Parents and primary caregivers of young children, including low-income, Black, Latine, Indigenous, immigrant, rural and urban families in three states.
observations.counterinterpretation: Using multiple arrangements may reflect preference and relational richness as well as constraint; the report does not treat portfolio care as inherently deficient or formal care as inherently superior.

observations.period: May-November 2024 interviews; constraints shaping care choices

affordability.value: cost was a primary factor for every parent interviewed and circumscribed both the type and frequency of care used

trust.value: most parents described trust as a driving factor, including whether care reinforced family language and culture

practical_constraints.value: location, hours and availability also shaped choices for some families

observations.method: Semi-structured interviews about care decisions, experiences, supports, desired arrangements and policy needs.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not assign relative causal weights to cost, trust, availability, location, hours, language or culture, and themes are not prevalence estimates.
observations.subgroup: Families with limited resources and varied formal, informal, cultural and geographic care networks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Affordability and trust can reinforce each other: a lower-cost arrangement may be chosen because it is trusted, while an expensive arrangement may still be rejected if relational or cultural fit is weak.

observations.period: May-November 2024 interviews; paid leave and return-to-work pressure

paid_leave_use.unit: parents reporting any paid leave after a child’s birth; only 8 reported using paid leave for a birth in the United States

early_return.value: many parents returned to work earlier than they wanted because they lacked paid leave or financial support

parental_time_want.value: most interviewed parents wanted substantially more time with their children after birth and later in the early years

observations.method: Interview reconstruction of care arrangements, parental work changes, leave, financial support and desired alternatives.
observations.uncertainty: Counts describe this purposive interview sample and cannot estimate the national rate of paid-leave access or early return to work.
observations.subgroup: Parents and primary caregivers, including workers in child care, home health and other low-wage or care-intensive occupations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some parents may prefer earlier work or shared care; the report's mechanism is that policy and income constraints narrowed the set of feasible choices for many interviewed families.

observations.period: May-November 2024 interviews; formal and informal care in families' actual and desired portfolios

formal_care_use.unit: parents reporting use of early care and education at some point before kindergarten

family_friend_neighbor_use.unit: parents reporting use of family, friend or neighbor care at some point

formal_care_want.unit: parents indicating they would ideally use formal early care and education before kindergarten; most wanted full-time care, while 11 preferred less than full-time

observations.method: Interview-based inventory of actual arrangements and unconstrained ideal arrangements; categories can overlap because families combined forms of care.
observations.uncertainty: The counts are not mutually exclusive, are based on a purposive sample, and describe reported experience rather than quality or developmental outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Families using or considering parental care, formal early education, and family, friend or neighbor care.
observations.counterinterpretation: The gap between use and ideal does not imply that formal care is unwanted; families often want all three forms, but with more parental time and better-supported quality and sequencing.

related_sources.claim: CSSP report page describing the qualitative research scope, publication date and report purpose.

boundary: This record captures a qualitative mechanism: families combine and sequence care arrangements, and affordability, trust, cultural fit, availability, work design and leave shape the gap between care used and care desired. It is not a nationally representative survey, prevalence estimate, causal evaluation, child-outcome study or universal preference model.
